hints: Start by asking why normal human cells cannot divide forever. Think about what happens to the telomeres at the ends of chromosomes each time DNA is replicated.
Recall which specific enzyme can rebuild telomeres, and remember it is normally switched off in most body cells but switched back on in cancer cells.
walkthrough:
**Recall why normal cells have a division limit**

Normal cells lose a little bit of telomere DNA at every division. This is the end-replication problem, because DNA polymerase cannot fully copy the very ends of linear chromosomes.

After many divisions the telomeres get critically short, and the cell stops dividing or dies. That limits normal cells to about 50 divisions.

**Recall how telomeres can be rebuilt**

The enzyme telomerase adds back the repeated DNA sequences to telomeres. It maintains telomere length so chromosomes are protected.

In most human somatic cells the gene for telomerase is switched off, so telomeres shorten. In stem cells and in cancer cells it can be active.

**Apply this to cancer cells**

Cancer cells divide far more times than normal cells because they are able to synthesise telomerase. This rebuilds their telomeres each cycle and prevents the shortening that would normally stop division.

So the correct statement is that they can make telomerase, which gives them effectively unlimited cell divisions.

options.A: Correct. Cancer cells often reactivate the telomerase gene, so they synthesise telomerase and maintain their telomeres through many divisions.
options.B: False. Telomere shortening is not caused by hydrolysis, and is not avoided by a mutation in the telomere DNA itself. It is caused by the inability of DNA polymerase to replicate chromosome ends.
options.C: False. All dividing human cells have DNA polymerase for semi-conservative replication, but DNA polymerase alone still cannot prevent telomere loss at the ends.
options.D: False. Cancer cells use telomerase to maintain telomere length and prevent loss, not to keep continuously increasing the number of repeats to longer and longer telomeres.
